title: How your childhood & personality can influence your fitness goals & training
summary: A psychological reflection: childhood shapes physique goals (ex-chubby kids chase shredded looks, small kids like him chase mass), which can feed dysmorphia and extreme dieting; personality shapes the best training style (his serious, industrious nature suits long high-volume sessions). Listen to your instincts and train in the way that matches who you are rather than chasing fads.

claims.claim: People who were chubby as kids tend to chase a shredded, striated physique, while small kids like him chase a massive, muscular one.
These childhood-driven goals also suggest which training and diet suit you, for pure bodybuilding.
Every lifter will encounter some muscle dysmorphia, which can be debilitating for mental health.
Chasing a childhood ideal can push you to extremes: ex-fat people may over-diet or starve; those who always wanted to be big may overeat and be unhealthy, as he once did.
Know why you lift; if the reason is personal and tied to your past, make sure it stays a healthy pursuit.
He is serious and industrious, likes long high-volume sessions where he loses himself in the task, doesn't mind training three hours, and has gotten his best results that way.
More active, dynamic personalities may do better with high intensity, shorter sessions (about 1.5 hours), less volume and more aggressive weight selection.

Training that matches your personality tends to give the best gains, partly from enthusiasm and consistency, but he thinks there is more correlation and that studies exist matching personality types to training regimens.
Listen to your instinct: if a training style feels right and matches who you are, keep doing it even if it isn't the latest fad or most scientifically optimal.
Many people succumb to the hype of new training methods and lose sight of who they are and why they started.
You build your body for yourself: disregard others, stay in touch with the teenager who started lifting, and embrace being serious or aloof.
